oralTraditions.claim: Tiramaghan Traoré, general to Soundiata and conqueror of Kaabu, is given as the eponymous ancestor of the Tarawele clan in the epic.
oralTraditions.transcription: Niane, Djibril Tamsir, Soundjata ou l'épopée mandingue, 1960

oralTraditions.claim: In the epic, two brothers who are both Traoré, Oulamba the elder and Oulani the younger, bring the buffalo woman of the land of Do to King Naré Maghan Kon Fatta, before the birth of Soundiata. When the younger brother has killed the buffalo, the elder composes a song in its glory and the younger cries out: "Brother, if you were a griot, no one could resist you." According to the tradition, this is where Traoré and Diabaté (Dioubaté) part ways: the same family divides into hunters and griots.
oralTraditions.transcription: Niane, Djibril Tamsir, Soundjata ou l'épopée mandingue, 1960

linguisticReconstructions.claim: The jamu is a patrilineal clan name: it designates membership in a descent group, not individual filiation to the father.
The Mande form of the name is Tarawele; Traoré is its francophone colonial transcription. No etymology commands consensus.

The name enters into a system of correspondences between family names of different peoples, established after Soundiata: in Wolof country, a Traoré is received as a brother by the Diop and may take their name, and reciprocally. The jamu is therefore not only hereditary, it is convertible from one area to another.

Before Soundiata, the Traoré occupy part of the country of Kiri, but the majority of them settle in the province that will later take the name Gangaran, north-west of Bouré. This territory is distinct from the cradle of the Keita, located around Dakadiala, Naréna and Kiri.

It is doubtful that the ancestor Tiramagan, celebrated as a general of Soundiata and founder of Kaabu, refers to a historical person: in Kaabu, where the narrative almost ignores his link with Soundiata, his name Tiramagan or Siramagan could designate the "chief of the ordeals", an object of worship, the lance of the ordeal, turned into a character. This reading is a hypothesis and does not command consensus; another reading sees in him a general sent by Soundiata.

For a foreigner, the jamu is the gateway into the social fabric: in Bamako, a Mandinka jamu is assigned to the newcomer to give them a place in the group. Today, the historical references of the pacts between names are often forgotten and people struggle to explain their origin.

casteOrSocialFunction.value: Status varies from one area to another, and this is not an absence of status. Traoré is among the jamuw hɔrɔn, of free and non-artisanal condition; the dictionary of jamuw records for the same entry hɔ́rɔn, then tontigi among the Bamana and the Maninka, then nùmu (blacksmith) among the Kagoro and the Wassoulounké. The numu side of the jamu is therefore attested, and the absence of a hereditary function does not hold for the whole area of the name.

sources.title: EthniAfrica — fiche du peuple Bambara, organisation clanique
sources.notes: Taken from the "Clan organisation" chapter of the Bambara people's fiche.

sources.title: Soundjata ou l'épopée mandingue
sources.notes: Niane, Djibril Tamsir, Présence Africaine, 1960. Transcription of the narrative of the griot Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté of Djeliba Koro (Siguiri). Reference source for the Soundiata epic and the lineages it founds; it is a written record of an oral tradition, not an archival document.

sources.title: Beyond the Mali Empire — A New Paradigm for the Sunjata Epic
sources.notes: Jansen, Jan, Universiteit Leiden. Critical work on the transmission of the epic and on the jamu as a social institution rather than as historical memory; used here for the nature of the jamu, not to date an ancestor.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Onomastic annex of the Bamadaba, an electronic Bambara-French dictionary supplementing the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA); the annex of clan names is identified as such by Vydrin, "Vers une lexicographie mandingue sur la base de grands corpus annotés", Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. 375 entries in MDF format, consulted in the complete file. The file provides no legend of its markers, and the reading adopted is the one the file imposes: \ca carries the Mandinka status terms themselves (nùmu, jèli, hɔ́rɔn, garanke, finɛ, tontigi, wage, gesere); \sn is read as senankun because the entry Kúyate annotates its own line "\sn Keyita" with a reservation stating that this relation is a friendly understanding and not a senankuya. The \sn links are not systematically reciprocal from one entry to another: each pair is therefore cited according to the entry that carries it, named in the claim or the gap. The entry Tàrawéle carries the group markers b (Bambara) and m, read as a Malinke indication by cross-checking with the entry Kéyità, which another of our fiches documents as a Malinke jamu; its \sn links name Jàra, Kɔ́nɛ, Jawara and Turɛ, and its variants are Traore and Taraore.

sources.title: A Guide to the Jembe
sources.notes: Charry, Eric, Percussive Notes 34(2), April 1996, pp. 66-72; the author is the ethnomusicologist of Mande Music (University of Chicago Press, 2000). Article from a specialist magazine, not a peer-reviewed journal: it is cited here for the attribution of jamuw to Mande social statuses (numu, jeli, horon), which he states by name clan by clan, and not for the history of the djembe.

sources.title: General History of Africa, IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century
sources.notes: UNESCO, General History of Africa, vol. IV, ed. D. T. Niane, 1984; consulted on the full text of the digitised copy, not on an index. Chapter 6, "Mali and the second Mandingo expansion" (D. T. Niane, pp. 117-171), gives lineage by lineage the settlement of the Malinke clans: the Kamara holding Sibi and Tabon and the Traoré the Gangaran (p. 127), the two Camara branches led by Tabon-Wana and Kamadian Camara of Sibi (p. 131), Tiramaghan Traoré founder of Gabu (p. 127 n. 28, p. 133), the correspondence of clan names from one people to another — a Traoré is received as a brother by the Diop in Wolof country and may take their name (p. 134 n. 43) —, the Diabaté griots of Keyla and the seven-yearly re-roofing of the Kamablon of Kangaba (p. 127 n. 28), and the griot of the mansa always chosen from the Kouyaté clan (p. 160). The work is a scholarly synthesis, not a chronicle: the claims it carries here are therefore classed outside writtenChronicles.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, number 38, 2002, pp. 175-197. Field survey in Mali. She sets out what the pact requires: the relationship holds in perpetuity for the whole descent of both lineages, marriage between them is prohibited — variously applied today, she notes — and mutual aid is owed without reservation. Cited for the obligation itself; it does not name the pair in this fiche, which is carried by the entries cited alongside it.

sources.title: Le Mali et la deuxième expansion manden
sources.notes: Niane, Djibril Tamsir, Histoire générale de l'Afrique, tome IV, chapitre 6, UNESCO/NEA, 1985; reproduction consulted on 23 September 2026, which covers the text only from p. 141. Confirms, in the French edition, what the English edition of this same chapter (gha-iv-mali) already gives: the Traoré in Gangaran (pp. 151-152), Tiramaghan Traoré founder of Gabu (p. 151, note 27), and the clan correspondence between Traoré and Diop established after the victory of Kirina (pp. 157-158, note 44). The cradle of the Keita — Dakadiala, Naréna and Kiri (p. 152, note 28) — is that of the Keita clan, distinct from the Gangaran of the Traoré.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, number 184, 2006, p. 687 and following. Cited for the warning it carries: the idea that joking kinship would ease conflicts is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict-resolution studies, thus as a discourse to be analysed and not as a measured effect. The starting page is verified, the ending page is not.

gaps.reason: Traoré and Tarawele are two spellings of the same jamu, the first stemming from the colonial transcription; the dictionary of jamuw adds a third, Taraore, under the same entry. It further groups Sane, Mane, Ouédraogo, Dembélé, Diouf and — at Ségou — Touré among its equivalences, clan names of other peoples held to be the same, an institution that the General History of Africa describes for its part by noting that a Traoré settled in Wolof country may take the name Diop. Neither the spellings nor the equivalences make separate lineages: none is treated as a homonym.
